entities.evidence: יַהְוֶה names the God who speaks to Cain, matching the LORD source tag.
Yahweh addresses Cain and calls Abel his brother, identifying the son born to Eve in Genesis 4:1.
The phrase “your brother” identifies Abel as Cain’s brother, introduced in Genesis 4:2.

name_review_base.evidence: יַהְוֶה names the God who speaks to Cain, matching the LORD source tag.
Yahweh addresses Cain and calls Abel his brother, identifying the son born to Eve in Genesis 4:1.
The phrase “your brother” identifies Abel as Cain’s brother, introduced in Genesis 4:2.

analysis.evidence: יַהְוֶה is the speaker, אֶל קַיִן identifies Cain as the addressee, and אֵי הֶבֶל אָחִיךָ gives the words spoken, “Where is Abel your brother?”
analysis.morphology: Qal wayyiqtol, third masculine singular, with prefixed וַ־

analysis.evidence: In וַיֹּאמֶר יַהְוֶה אֶל קַיִן, “Yahweh said to Cain,” יַהְוֶה names the speaker who asks Cain where his brother Abel is.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular proper noun without prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: Personal name of the God of Israel

draft.change: Add Gen.9.8 as evidence for the existing addressee sense of אֶל at word index 0.
draft.definition: With a verb of speaking, אֶל introduces the addressee.
draft.evidence: In Gen.9.8, וְאֶל בָּנָיו adds Noah’s sons to the hearers already introduced by אֶל נֹחַ.

analysis.evidence: In וַיֹּאמֶר יַהְוֶה אֶל קַיִן, אֶל introduces Cain as the person Yahweh asks, “Where is Abel your brother?”
analysis.sense: Marks the person or people addressed.

draft.change: Add a personal-name article for Cain with its etymology left open pending evidence.
draft.definition: Cain, the son of Adam and Eve and brother of Abel.
draft.evidence: Genesis 4:1 names Eve’s son קַיִן. Genesis 4:2 identifies Abel as his brother and names Cain again when describing his work.

analysis.evidence: וַיֹּאמֶר יַהְוֶה אֶל קַיִן names Cain as the person YHWH addresses. In the question אֵי הֶבֶל אָחִיךָ, “Where is Abel your brother?”, the suffix on אָחִיךָ identifies Abel as Cain’s brother.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular proper noun, with no prefix or suffix. The separate preposition אֶל introduces Cain as the addressee.
analysis.sense: The personal name of Abel’s brother.

draft.change: Add the interrogative particle אֵי as a separate word under the consonantal key אי. The existing noun אִי means “island, coastland.”
draft.definition: אֵי introduces a question asking where someone or something is.
draft.evidence: In Genesis 4:9 Yahweh asks Cain where Abel is. Cain replies that he does not know and asks whether he is his brother’s keeper.

analysis.evidence: In אֵי הֶבֶל אָחִיךָ, “Where is Abel your brother?”, הֶבֶל אָחִיךָ identifies the person and אֵי asks his whereabouts. Cain answers לֹא יָדַעְתִּי, “I do not know.”
analysis.morphology: Interrogative particle of place, without prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: Asks where someone or something is.

analysis.evidence: YHWH asks Cain אֵי הֶבֶל אָחִיךָ, “Where is Abel, your brother?” The appositive אָחִיךָ identifies Abel as Cain’s brother.
In אֵי הֶבֶל אָחִיךָ, “Where is Abel, your brother?”, אָחִיךָ stands in apposition to Abel. The suffix refers to Cain, whom YHWH addresses.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular construct noun with a second-person masculine singular possessive suffix.

analysis.evidence: After יַהְוֶה asks Cain where Abel is, the second וַיֹּאמֶר introduces Cain’s reply. Its subject is Cain, whose first words are לֹא יָדַעְתִּי (“I do not know”).
analysis.morphology: Qal wayyiqtol, third person masculine singular, with prefixed וַ־ and no suffix

analysis.evidence: In לֹא יָדַעְתִּי, “I do not know,” לֹא negates יָדַעְתִּי. Cain denies knowing where Abel is.
analysis.morphology: Uninflected negative particle with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: YHWH asks אֵי הֶבֶל אָחִיךָ, “Where is Abel your brother?” Cain replies לֹא יָדַעְתִּי, “I do not know.” The question supplies the understood complement, “where Abel is.”
analysis.morphology: Qal perfect, first person common singular, with the subject ending ־תִּי.

analysis.evidence: Asked where Abel is, Cain replies הֲשֹׁמֵר אָחִי אָנֹכִי, “Am I my brother’s keeper?” The prefix הֲ marks the question, and שֹׁמֵר identifies the person who would watch over Abel.
analysis.morphology: Interrogative הֲ prefixed to a Qal active participle, masculine singular, used substantivally.

analysis.evidence: YHWH calls Abel הֶבֶל אָחִיךָ, “Abel your brother.” Cain refers to Abel as אָחִי, “my brother,” when he asks, “Am I my brother’s keeper?”
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular construct noun with the first-person singular possessive suffix ־ִי.

analysis.evidence: Cain asks הֲשֹׁמֵר אָחִי אָנֹכִי, “Am I my brother’s keeper?” The final אָנֹכִי refers to Cain and serves as the subject of the predicate שֹׁמֵר אָחִי, “my brother’s keeper.”
analysis.morphology: Independent personal pronoun, first person common singular
